en: The Sūtra Spoken by the Buddha on the Bodhisattva Ocean-Mountain Wisdom, Chapter One:
Liberation. The Sūtra of Avalokana on the Body of Amitābha Buddha Awakening the Great Assembly. Chapter One: Liberation.
Thus have I heard. At one time, the Buddha was staying in the kingdom of Karmavardhana, together with a great assembly of eight [thousand] bhikṣus.
Together with ten thousand people,
he attained realization through the practices of his original conduct of great wisdom;
his name was Bodhisattva Avalokiteśvara.
Mahāsthāmaprāpta Bodhisattva,
Bhaiṣajyarāja Bodhisattva,
and Bhaiṣajyasamudgata Bodhisattva.
Samantabhadra Bodhisattva,
Dharmeśvararāja Bodhisattva,
and Siṃhanāda Bodhisattva.
Dhāraṇī Bodhisattva,
Ākāśagarbha Bodhisattva,
and Guṇakośa Bodhisattva.
Bodhisattva Ratnagarbha,
Bodhisattva Suvarṇagarbha,
and Bodhisattva Vajragarbha.
The Bodhisattva King of Radiance,
the Bodhisattva Ocean and Mountain Wisdom,
and the Bodhisattva King of the Flower Adornment.
The Bodhisattva Jewel King,
the Bodhisattva Moonlight King,
and the Bodhisattva Sunlight King.
Samādhirāja Bodhisattva,
Samādhy-vaśavartirāja Bodhisattva,
and Maheśvararāja Bodhisattva.
The Bodhisattva Śvetaketu-rāja,
the Bodhisattva Mahāteja-rāja,
and the Bodhisattva Anantagātra.
These twenty-five bodhisattva-mahāsattvas had all attained such mastery.
At that time, there were also eight thousand śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas.
Furthermore, there were twenty thousand Brahma kings and Mahesvara kings;
additionally, there were twelve thousand powerful mantra-holding kings and forty-eight thousand dragon kings.
Furthermore, there were ten trillion rākṣasa kings,
as well as two thousand seers possessing the five supernatural powers,
and eighty-four thousand kings of the Sumeru mountains.
As well as the dragon kings of rivers, seas, and waters;
and the bhikṣus, bhikṣuṇīs, upāsakas, and upāsikās—
all such members of the eightfold assembly were present within the gathering.
They sat together to listen to the Dharma.
At that time, the World-Honored One was at the site of enlightenment beneath the Bodhi tree made of the seven precious gems.
That bodhi tree was four hundred thousand yojanas high.
At that time, the Tathāgata sat upon the lion Dharma-seat and turned the great wheel of Dharma for the great assembly.
He rained down the great rain of the Dharma,
preaching the dharmas of meditative concentration, liberation, and escape from the eight difficulties.
While he was preaching this Dharma,
Heavenly rain fell of seven-jeweled flowers.
At that time, the Tathāgata emitted a great radiance from the crown of his head,
in shades of blue, yellow, white, and red.
It shone upward upon the Heaven of the Thirty-three and downward upon the eighteen hells,
causing the earth to quake in six ways.
What are called the six kinds of earthquakes? They are:

the shaking of the heavens, the shaking of the earth, the shaking of the great oceans, the shaking of the mountains, the shaking of the grasses, trees, and sentient beings, and the shaking of all the hells.
For this reason, it is called the sixfold earthquake.
When the Tathāgata emits light,
those in the hells and the hungry ghosts all attain liberation.
"Except for the icchantikas,
who cannot attain liberation.
At that time, the bhikṣu Ānanda rose from his seat.
In the midst of the great assembly, he praised the Buddha with these verses:
The World-Honored One of Great Compassion, Sovereign of all dharmas, Appeared in this world to deliver beings from the stream of birth and death.
The Buddha is like a vajra-jewel; there is no one who does not rejoice.
Therefore, all you great assemblies, now join your palms in prostration. Today we have encountered the Vajra Jewel;
like those with blind eyes who have gained sight of the sun and moon, and like the Kings of the Sun and Moon who can dispel the darkness of birth and death, it is like the King of Wind and Fire.
He burns away all evils, like a compassionate parent who, seeing their child with a grave illness,
harbors sorrow and distress day and night. Thinking of the Unsurpassed Teacher,

the World-Honored One of Great Compassion appearing in the world to extensively deliver beings from the flow of birth and death— having obtained the sight of the World-Honored One, [one is liberated].
"There is none who is not liberated; therefore, O great assembly, you should wish to behold the Unsurpassed Honored One.
At that time, Ānanda, having finished praising and reciting for the Buddha, [fell silent].
He addressed the Buddha, saying:
"World-Honored One,
this is the method for all sentient beings to contemplate the body."
"What is that matter?
I only pray that the World-Honored One will explain it to me.
The Buddha told Ānanda:
Listen attentively, listen attentively!
I shall now explain it for you.
As for the method of contemplating the body:
One should maintain right concentration of body and mind.
When body and mind are concentrated, all dharmas are concentrated;
when all dharmas are concentrated, all phenomena are likewise concentrated.
If one wishes for all phenomena to be concentrated,
then both body and mind must be concentrated; when both body and mind are concentrated, [the phenomena will be so].
He did not look east or west;
he did not look north or south;
he did not look toward the four intermediate directions.
One does not observe what is above or below;
one does not observe empty space;
one does not observe external conditions.
One does not contemplate internal conditions;
one does not contemplate the physical form of the body;
one does not contemplate forms or sounds.
Do not observe the conduct of others;
do not observe the bodies of others.
Observe only your own body and do not observe the faults of others.
One should simply observe one's own conduct and not observe external forms;
one observes only the objectless.
If one can thus observe one's own body, [one attains liberation].
There are no external objects;
there is only the out-breath and only the in-breath.
If one is able to know this counting of the breath,
the practitioner should be given the method for maintaining the body and should be given the method for contacting the body.
One should apply the method for the "Heated Summit.
If one can contemplate the body in this manner,
this constitutes the authentic and true method for contemplating the body.
Setting aside this contemplation of the body,
if one searches thoroughly throughout the ten directions and in every place,
there is no other dharma by which liberation can be attained.
At that time, Ānanda again addressed the Buddha, saying:
"World-Honored One,
if one can contemplate the body in this way while sitting..."
"What samādhi has he attained that he possesses such merit?
The Buddha said:
Excellent, excellent!
You have now posed this question.
Listen attentively, listen attentively.
Reflect upon this well;
I shall explain it for you.
O bhikṣus and bhikṣuṇīs!
If there are faithful laymen or faithful laywomen who purely maintain their precepts and refrain from committing any evil deeds.
Diligently cultivate meditative concentration (*dhyāna*).
Having attained meditative concentration, one will not provide an opportunity for the various Māras to gain advantage.
There shall be five types of concentration.
What are the five concentrations?
They are the concentration of śrāvakas, the concentration of pratyekabuddhas, the concentration of arhats, the concentration of bodhisattvas, and the concentration of buddhas.
One attains these five concentrations.
Furthermore, there are five eyes.
What are the five eyes?
They are the eye of the śrāvaka, the eye of the pratyekabuddha, the eye of the arhat, the eye of the bodhisattva, and the eye of the buddha.
Having attained these five eyes,
there are further five sciences.
What are the five sciences?
They possess the illumination of the śrāvakas, the illumination of the pratyekabuddhas, the illumination of the arhats, the illumination of the bodhisattvas, and the illumination of the Buddhas.
Having attained these five illuminations,
they further attain the five supernormal powers.
What are the five supernormal powers?

They are the supernormal power of the śrāvaka, the supernormal power of the pratyekabuddha, the supernormal power of the arhat, the supernormal power of the bodhisattva, and the supernormal power of the buddhas.
One attains these five supernormal powers.
Furthermore, there are five kinds of penetration.
What are the five penetrations?
They are the penetration of the śrāvakas, the penetration of the pratyekabuddhas, the penetration of the arhats, the penetration of the bodhisattvas, and the penetration of the buddhas.
Having attained these five penetrations,
there are furthermore five knowledges.
What are the five knowledges?
The wisdom of śrāvakas, the wisdom of pratyekabuddhas, the wisdom of arhats, the wisdom of bodhisattvas, and the wisdom of all buddhas—
having attained these five wisdoms,
there are further five types of insight.
What are the five kinds of wisdom?
They are the wisdom of śrāvakas, the wisdom of pratyekabuddhas, the wisdom of arhats, the wisdom of bodhisattvas, and the wisdom of all buddhas.
One attains these five kinds of wisdom.
By understanding all phenomena, one comprehends all meanings.
Furthermore, there are three kinds of impermanence.
What are these three kinds of impermanence?
All sentient beings are impermanent; śrāvakas are impermanent; pratyekabuddhas are impermanent.
Having understood these three kinds of impermanence, one further understands that there are three kinds of permanence.
What is the permanence of the three existences?
It is the permanence of the Buddhas, the permanence of the Bodhisattvas, and the permanence of the Dharma and Sangha;
to attain these three kinds of permanence.
Furthermore, they are able to uphold the True Dharma;
by upholding the True Dharma, they are further able to constantly delight in meditative concentration (*dhyāna*);
having attained this meditative concentration, they further attain the four *dhyānas*.
Having attained these four dhyānas, one should accordingly observe the phenomena within one's own body.
By observing the phenomena within the body, one becomes detached from afflictions;
through detachment from afflictions, one develops self-disgust for the body.
By revulsion toward the body, one immediately attains the body of an arhat;
by attaining the body of an arhat, one attains the body of a bodhisattva;
and by attaining the body of a bodhisattva, one further attains the vajra-samādhi.
Having attained the Vajra-samādhi, one obtains the Dharma-body, the eternal body, the vajra-body, the indestructible body, the body of boundless bliss, and the ever-abiding body.
The Buddha said to Ānanda:
Regarding what you have just asked concerning this contemplation of the body while seated:
what samādhi is attained,
and what are its merits?
"It is as I have said;
the meaning is thus.
At that time, Ānanda—
Again, he addressed the Buddha, saying:
"World-Honored One,
setting aside the merit of sitting in meditation and the merit of reciting the sutras..."
"What is that matter?
The Buddha told Ānanda,
"There is one who is able to read and recite a single four-line verse."
The merit is immeasurable, boundless, and inconceivable.
Furthermore, Ānanda,
if there should be a Dharma-preacher...
He is well able to explain the meaning.
His merit is likewise immeasurable, boundless, and inconceivable.
Ānanda addressed the Buddha:
"What are the merits of giving?
The Buddha told Ānanda:
'If there is one who can joyfully relinquish wealth for even a single thought-moment...'"
The merit is immeasurable, boundless, and inconceivable.
Furthermore, Ānanda,
listen again now.
If there were another person who bestowed food, drink, and clothing upon a hundred thousand sentient beings,
it would not equal the merit of making offerings to a single sick bhikṣu, which is immeasurable and boundless.
Setting this matter aside,
suppose there were another person who practiced the giving of chariots and horses, liberating ten trillion sentient beings;
this would not equal the immeasurable and boundless merit of a person who erects a stupa or monastery and makes offerings to three bhikṣus.
Setting this matter aside,
suppose there were another person who bestowed hundreds of thousands of treasuries as alms upon the sentient beings of a single world-system;
this would not equal the merit of another person who gives rise to a single thought of wholesome resolve.
If one directs the mind toward the Buddha and listens to the Dharma for even a single moment or a single thought-instant,
that person’s merit will be immeasurable, boundless, and inconceivable;
it is entirely the great cause, the great fruit, and the great retribution of supreme Bodhi.
At that time, Ānanda again addressed the Buddha, saying:
"World-Honored One."
If there are bhikṣus, bhikṣuṇīs, upāsakas, or upāsikās who are able to give rise to even a single thought of a wholesome mind,
will they possess the cause for bodhi in future lives?
My mind is currently unable to comprehend this;
I only pray that the World-Honored One will explain it to me.
The Buddha told Ānanda:
"In my view of the conventional truth,
I see that while all sentient beings attain naturalness through faith in the Buddha, it is difficult to attain the Way without such faith."
For what reason? It is,
for example, like a person who constantly harbors unwholesome thoughts and slanders bhikṣus,
giving rise to arbitrary discrimination regarding whether they possess virtue or lack it.
Because they give rise to the mark of slander,
one should know that such persons will certainly fall into the state of mind of hell;
it is likewise for those who slander the True Dharma.
At that time, having heard the Buddha speak these words,
Ānanda immediately rose from his seat.
He prostrated with his head at the Buddha's feet and addressed him, saying,
"World-Honored One."
I only pray that you will explain this in detail for the great assembly. Why is this?
Because if it is explained extensively...
From this day forward, we shall have no further doubt. Why is this?
Because it has been spoken thus.
Open my ears and eyes. Why is this?
It is like a blind person seeing various forms and images.
It is like a deaf person hearing a sound;
it is like a condemned prisoner led to the marketplace for execution when the Great Sovereign King’s sudden pardon arrives.
That person was revived and immediately cried out:
"How wonderful!"
"I have now regained this life," he said,
and further added, "From this day forward,
we too shall resolve to attain the sublime mind of unsurpassed bodhi."
He spoke again, saying:
"If I do not now resolve to attain bodhicitta,
you should know that my body is no different from that of an ox."
Ānanda said to the Buddha,
“This person has been able to give rise to a wholesome mind because of these painful matters; therefore,
I have now questioned you on this account.”
World-Honored One,
all sentient beings also give rise to the virtuous mind of unsurpassed bodhi; therefore,
from this day forward, there shall be no further doubt.
A hundred thousand sentient beings all gave rise to the virtuous mind of unsurpassed bodhi.
At that time, the World-Honored One again addressed Ānanda:
"Observe only your own body."
The power of goodness is spontaneous; right mindfulness is spontaneous;
the True Dharma is spontaneous; liberation is spontaneous;
samādhi is spontaneous; and nirvāṇa is spontaneous.
Why is this? It is like a person who, through diligence and a straightforward mind, attains right liberation and is immediately reborn in heaven;
yet that person does not seek liberation.
Liberation will naturally arrive;
do not seek birth in the heavens,
for birth in the heavens will naturally arrive.
Why is this? It is, for example,
like a person who encounters the chaos and ruin of a nation,
losing their land and fleeing far away to another country.
Though he is bound to others,
this person remembers his parents at every breath, never letting go of them in his mind.
From time to time, this person further reflects to himself, saying:
"I have now lost my native land and am far removed from my parents, with no means of seeing them.
Furthermore, I thought to myself:
'For now, let me observe my own body.'"
"I am now subject to another and have no means of liberation;
there is only the unsurpassed great power of the Triple Gem.
At that time, this person no longer directs their thoughts outward.
Even if one carves an image from wood and worships it day after day,
never ceasing for a moment.
Maintaining such right mindfulness for one year, two years, or even up to three years,
through the natural power of his wholesome merit from thus performing prostrations, he suddenly returned to his own country and saw his parents.
He felt immeasurable joy.
The Buddha told Ānanda,
"In truth, that wood possesses no power of its own."
"This is simply brought about by the power of the wholesome roots resulting from right mindfulness.
The right mindfulness and liberation of sentient beings in the world are likewise so.
At that time, Ānanda again addressed the Buddha, saying:
World-Honored One,
if the sentient beings of the world were able to attain liberation through such right mindfulness,
there would be rebirth in heaven for all, and not a single hell or realm of hungry ghosts.
The Buddha told Ānanda:

"That sentient beings in the world fail to attain liberation or rebirth in heaven is entirely due to their abundance of falsehood and paucity of reality, lacking even a single moment of right mindfulness."
For these reasons,
those in hell are many,
while those who attain liberation are few.
Why is this? It is like a person who, toward their own parents and preceptors,
manifests filial piety outwardly while harboring impiety within.
For such evil persons, although the retribution has not yet arrived, its arrival is not far off.
The sentient beings of the world manifest diligence outwardly,
while inwardly harboring insincerity.
They slander the True Dharma;
although the retribution has not yet been meted out, the path ahead is not far off.
The world abounds in the empty and lacks the real.
Lacking right mindfulness,
one likewise fails to attain liberation.
The Buddha told Ānanda:
"According to what you have just said, all sentient beings should also be liberated.
As I have explained, such is the case."
At that time, Ānanda addressed the Buddha, saying:
"World-Honored One,
by cultivating what roots of goodness does one attain right liberation?"
The Buddha told Ānanda:
"Listen well now, and contemplate with right mindfulness.
I shall now explain to you ten ways of rebirth."
What are the ten ways of rebirth?
First, one contemplates the body with right mindfulness and constantly maintains a sense of joy.
First, having offered food, drink, and clothing to the Buddha and the Sangha,
one will be reborn in the Land of Amitābha.
Second, with right mindfulness, one offers sweet and excellent medicinal herbs to a single sick bhikṣu and to all sentient beings.
Third, through right mindfulness, one does not harm even a single life and maintains compassion for all beings.
One shall be reborn in the Land of Amitābha.
Fourth, one will be reborn in the land of Amitābha by maintaining right mindfulness of the precepts received from the teacher,
cultivating pure wisdom and the holy life with a mind always filled with joy.
Fifth, one will be reborn in the land of Amitābha by maintaining right mindfulness and being filial toward one's parents,
and by showing reverence for one's teachers and elders.
Without harboring a mind of pride or rebellion,
one will be reborn in the land of Amitābha.
Sixth, with right mindfulness, one proceeds to the monastic quarters.
Revering stupas and monasteries,
inquiring into the Dharma to understand its single meaning,
one shall be reborn in the land of Amitābha.
Seventh, with right mindfulness, one should observe the eight precepts for one day and one night;
by observing them without breaking even a single precept for that day and night,
one will be reborn in the land of Amitābha.
Eighth, as for right mindfulness: if one can, during the months of fasting and on the days of fasting,
remain far removed from private dwellings and constantly approach virtuous teachers.
Reborn in the Land of Amitābha;
ninth, one should always maintain pure precepts with right mindfulness and diligently cultivate the joy of meditative concentration.
One who protects the Dharma does not engage in harsh speech.
If one can practice in this manner,
they will be reborn in the land of Amitābha.
Tenth, if one possesses right mindfulness regarding the unsurpassed path and does not give rise to a mind of slander,
but instead diligently maintains the pure precepts and further teaches those who lack wisdom to disseminate this Dharma of the sutra.
He awakened and transformed immeasurable multitudes;
all such persons as these attained rebirth [in that land].
At that time, Ānanda again addressed the Buddha, saying:
World-Honored One,
all sentient beings dwell in a world of ignorance;
they do not see the Buddhas of the past, the Buddhas of the future, or the Buddhas of the present.
“World-Honored One, this world of ignorance is itself hell.
To what should one turn for refuge?
What is called the root of precepts?”
"I only pray that the World-Honored One will explain this for us all.
The Buddha told Ānanda:
If all sentient beings, whether in the present, do not see the Buddhas of the past, the Buddhas of the future, or the Buddhas of the present,
they should always uphold the names of the Three Refuges.
What are called the Three Refuges?
One should speak these words:
"Namo Buddhāya, namo Dharmāya, namo Saṃghāya.
What does it mean to say "Namo Buddhāya, namo Dharmāya, namo Saṃghāya"?
To say "Namo Buddhāya" in the foreign tongue means taking refuge in the Buddha;
"Dharma" means taking refuge in the Dharma;
and "Saṃgha" means taking refuge in the Saṃgha.
These three refuges are the root of the precepts.
One should accept and uphold them in this way,
and recite them in this way.
Recalling in this way and contemplating correctly in this way,
one should know that such a person, in every life and birth, in every place and location, [will attain this].
By the power of the three refuges, one constantly attains right mindfulness and does not enter the evil realms;
all of this is due to the power of liberation through the three refuges.
The Buddha told Ānanda:
Regarding what you have just asked— concerning where all sentient beings dwelling in the world of ignorance should turn for refuge—
the meaning is exactly as I have explained.
At that time, Ānanda again addressed the Buddha,
saying: "World-Honored One,
if there are bhikṣus, bhikṣuṇīs, upāsakas, or upāsikās..."
To uphold this sutra,
to read and recite this sutra,
and to maintain right mindfulness of this sutra.
"What is this 'Cloud of Merit'?
The Buddha told Ānanda:
You have now asked an excellent question.
Listen attentively and reflect well upon it;
I shall now explain it for you.
If a person lacks roots of goodness, they shall not hear this sutra.
If a person lacks fundamental goodness, they shall not hear this Dharma.
If one belongs to the class of icchantikas, they shall not hear these words.
Those who possess pure precepts may now hear this sutra. Why is this?
This sutra can deliver one from the eight difficulties,
as well as from the hells, the hungry ghosts, the asuras, and others;
those who have broken the precepts or committed the five heinous crimes shall all be completely liberated.
"There is only one icchantika.
Ānanda addressed the Buddha,
"World-Honored One," he said.
In the past, I told Śāriputra:
"All sentient beings are my children;
there is no distinction between self and other."
"Why do you not deliver the icchantikas?
The Buddha told Ānanda,
"Listen attentively now."
"Can a corpse in this world be brought back to life?
Ānanda replied to the Buddha,
"World-Honored One, it is impossible for a corpse in this world to be brought back to life."
The Buddha said to Ānanda,
"It is likewise impossible for an icchantika to attain the Way.
Ānanda addressed the Buddha:
"How is it that a corpse in this world, having been dead for one day, two days, three days, four days, five days, six days,
or seven days, might yet come back to life?
The Buddha told Ānanda:
Regarding the precepts, there are those who, though like corpses for one day, two days, three days, four days, five days, six days, or seven days, may yet return to life;
these correspond respectively to the first, second, third, fourth, and fifth *ānantarya* (immediate) transgressions.
Such a person, though they have fallen into hell, immediately gives rise to a mind of repentance.
By the power of this wholesome force of repentance, they are immediately delivered from hell.
Such deliverance is like a corpse that returns to life after seven days.
One who cannot live for seven days is precisely an icchantika.
Why is this? Because an icchantika lacks roots of goodness.
For this reason, they are not saved.
The Buddha told Ānanda:
"Regarding what you asked just now—why the icchantikas are not saved—"
As I have taught, such is its meaning. Chapter Two:
Bodhisattvas Beholding Buddha-lands and Rebirth in Them. At that time, there was a bodhisattva among the assembly.
Named Sāgarabuddhivikrīḍitābhijña,
possessing majestic power and sovereignty with his renown reaching throughout the ten directions,
he rose from his seat amidst the great assembly.
Adjusting his robes, he paid homage to the Buddha and stepped forward to address him, saying,
"World-Honored One."
"Regarding all that which sentient beings cultivate and practice,
what merit is the most supreme?
The Buddha told Sāgarabuddhi:
Listen attentively now, listen attentively!
Reflect upon this well.
I shall now explain liberation for you.
If there are sentient beings who give food, drink, and clothing as alms to all sentient beings in a single world-system,
it would not equal the immeasurable, boundless, and inconceivable merit obtained by someone who, for even a moment, pays homage with right mindfulness.
Setting this matter aside,
if one were to perform prostrations for the rest of one's life,
it would not equal the greater merit of someone who lives out a single lifetime [in such practice].
Setting this matter aside,
even if someone were to save the lives of a hundred thousand beings,
it would not equal the merit of another person who, having once conceived a virtuous mind, constructs a stupa or monastery.
One may provide offerings through these four matters;
yet the merit of making offerings to the four types of śramaṇas is even greater.
Let us set this matter aside for a moment.
If there were someone who made offerings to hundreds of thousands of śramaṇas,
it would not equal the merit of another person who, having given rise to a single virtuous thought and harboring a heart of joy,
grants one person permission to leave the household life. The latter's merit is even greater.
Setting this matter aside,
if there were another person who ordained hundreds of thousands of people,
it would not equal the merit of someone who gives rise to a single thought of goodness.
Furthermore, if one stays amidst a great assembly and at one time hears the Dharma and understands the meaning of even one or two words,
the merit thereof is even greater. Setting that matter aside,
suppose there is another person who, staying amidst a great assembly, understands hundreds of thousands of meanings.
It is not as good as someone sitting in meditation with a settled mind; the merit of the bliss of meditative concentration is further immeasurable, boundless, and inconceivable.
Setting that matter aside, suppose there is another person in the world who hears hundreds of thousands of sūtras.
It is not as meritorious as for someone who aspires to hear the two words "Nirvāṇa" and "Eternal Abiding" from the Mahāvaipulya; its merit is immeasurable, boundless, and inconceivable. Why is this?
The two characters "Ever-Abiding" (nitya) are that which has been practiced and is the merit of all Buddhas of the three periods of time— past, future,
and present. Why is this so?
These two words can eliminate the heavy sins of birth and death— immeasurable and boundless— of sentient beings throughout the past, future, and present lives,
with the exception of those who hold to false views (icchantikas).
By eliminating these offenses, one attains true liberation and is immediately reborn in the land of Amitābha.
For this reason, the meaning and flavor of *nirvāṇa* are the most supreme among all merits.
The Buddha told Śāgaramati:
"Regarding what you have just said concerning all merits, which merit is the most supreme?
As I have taught:"
The meaning is thus.
At that time, the Bodhisattva Sāgarabuddhidhara again addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One,
what joys are there in that land of Amitābha Buddha such that all sentient beings wish to be born there?”
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed Śāgaramati:
"You should now arise,
join your palms, and straighten your body."
Facing west with right mindfulness, they contemplated the land of Amitābha and vowed to behold the Buddha Amitābha.
At that time, the entire great assembly saw the Bodhisattva Sāgarabuddhi rise and join his palms in reverence.
They all likewise rose and together gazed upon Amitābha Buddha.
At that time, Amitābha Buddha manifested great supernormal powers and a great radiance,
which illuminated the body of the Bodhisattva Śānasamudra.
At that time, the Bodhisattva Ocean-Mountain Wisdom immediately beheld all the magnificent and exquisite adornments of Amitābha’s land;
every world therein was adorned with the seven treasures.
All the lands are illuminated by the light of the seven treasures:

mountains of the seven treasures, grounds of the seven treasures, trees of the seven treasures, flowers of the seven treasures, stupas of the seven treasures, courtyards of the seven treasures, and ponds of the seven treasures.
There were waters of eight virtues, food of six flavors, and alms bowls of the seven treasures.
The sun and moon deities rained down flowers of the seven treasures and rained down garments of the seven treasures.
The various devas and ṛṣis perform all kinds of music.
That land of the Buddha Amitābha is pure and magnificently adorned;
nets of pure gold completely cover the buddha-field.
There is a world where all are adorned with jewel trees, most exquisite and supreme;
in that land, the sun, moon, and wheel of Dharma constantly revolve.
The people of that land do not practice external matters;
they practice only internal matters.
They do not practice false teachings.
One correctly practices the internal Dharma and does not practice external teachings;
one correctly studies the internal teaching.
One does not cultivate external meanings;
one correctly cultivates internal meanings.
One does not cultivate non-Buddhist paths.
One correctly cultivates the inner path and does not perceive external phenomena;
one possesses correct vision regarding internal phenomena.
He does not speak external languages;
he speaks only the internal language.
All sentient beings aged seven years and above take refuge in the True Dharma.
The mouth speaks the words of the Vaipulya;
the ears hear the sounds of the Vaipulya;
the mind understands the meaning of the Vaipulya.
At that time, the Bodhisattva Sāgarabuddhivikrīḍitābhijña saw Amitābha Buddha situated at the site of enlightenment beneath a bodhi tree made of the seven precious substances;
that bodhi tree was four hundred thousand yojanas in height.
Beneath it was a lion throne;
that lion throne was five hundred yojanas high,
and a net of pure gold completely covered its surface.
Amitābha Buddha sat upon the Dharma throne,
turning the Great Wheel of Dharma for the great assembly and raining down the great rain of Dharma.
He preached the Dharma of non-retrogression and rained down the great rain of Dharma;
he turned the wheel of the Dharma of non-retrogression.
When he beheld this scene, he also saw that within ten billion worlds and beyond the seas of ten billion worlds, ten billion Mount Sumerus were all entirely golden.
Amitābha Buddha manifested great supernormal powers and withdrew his radiance, so that the earth,
stones, and mountains of ten billion worlds were restored to their former state.
The Buddha told the Bodhisattva Ocean-Mountain Wisdom:
"As for what you have just asked— why it is that all sentient beings wish to be born in the land of Amitābha because of its wondrous joys—
it is exactly as you have perceived."
At that time, the Bodhisattva Sāgarabuddhi addressed the Buddha, saying:
"World-Honored One,
we now vow that all sentient beings shall be born in that land."
"Then we too wish to be born there.
The Buddha prophesied that those who possess right contemplation and right mindfulness will all attain right liberation and be born there.
Furthermore, O Śāgaramati:
"You who have now made such a vow are a great Bodhisattva Mahāsattva.
At that time, there was a Bodhisattva Mahāsattva among the assembly.
His original surname was Tola,
and his given name was Mahākāśyapa.
He possessed innate supernormal powers and exercised sovereign mastery over majestic virtue.
Having attained complete penetration into all phenomena,
he was always without fear;
rising from his seat in the midst of the great assembly, he joined his palms together.
On behalf of the assembly, he asked about certain matters, saying to the Buddha:
"World-Honored One,
the Tathāgata is the Dharma-King of great compassion for all sentient beings."
Universally covering all things, it emits a great radiance that illuminates every world throughout the ten directions.
How did the Bodhisattva Sāgaraprajñā come to behold Amitābha?
"How is it that all sentient beings do not see [the Tathāgata]?
One should know that, in reality, the Tathāgata has no equality.
The Buddha told Kāśyapa:
Listen attentively now.
It is like the sun and moon, which shine universally upon all things;
that the blind do not see them is not the fault of the sun and moon.
All sentient beings do not see [their own] heavy transgressions and afflictions;
the Tathāgata is likewise.
Furthermore, Kāśyapa, listen again now.
All sentient beings have not yet engaged in the bodhisattva practices;
therefore, they cannot be equal to a bodhisattva. Why is this?

The Bodhisattva possesses great kindness, great compassion, great goodness, great power, the great Dharma-treasury, great mindfulness, great vows, great causes, great conditions, the Great Vehicle, the Great Path, great joy, great relinquishment, and great pity that universally covers all.
Therefore, this is called the Great Practice of a Bodhisattva.
Furthermore, Kāśyapa, a Bodhisattva is further able to enter into hell for the sake of all sentient beings.
They do not consider it difficult to undergo great suffering and affliction;
they vow to deliver all who have committed offenses.
For this reason, it is called the Great Practice of a Bodhisattva.
The Buddha told Kāśyapa:
"The Bodhisattva Sāgarabuddhivikrīḍitābhijña possesses great majestic power and virtue in exactly this way.
The Buddha told Kāśyapa:
Regarding what you have just asked— how it is that bodhisattvas are able to see the Tathāgata while sentient beings do not—
the meaning is exactly as I have explained.
Kāśyapa addressed the Buddha:
"Excellent, excellent!
It is truly as the Holy Teaching declares."
World-Honored One,
by virtue of the Buddha’s spiritual power,
we are not ignorant of this matter.
It is for the sake of future sentient beings that I have asked about this meaning.
At that time, the Buddha told the Bodhisattva Ocean-Mountain Wisdom:
"If you now wish to deliver all sentient beings, you should receive, uphold, and recite this sutra."
The Bodhisattva Sāgarabuddhi addressed the Buddha, saying:
"World-Honored One,
what should this sutra be named?"
"How should it be upheld?
The Buddha told Śāṃudratīra:
"Listen well now."
This sutra is titled "The Sutra on the Samādhi of Liberation through Right Mindfulness of Contemplating the Body Spoken for the Great Assembly by Amitābha.
Its second name is "Crossing Over the Various Existential Currents, Birth-and-Death, and the Eight Difficulties."
The three [Buddhas] preached the Dharma for the last time to deliver sentient beings with whom they had a karmic connection;
the Tathāgata received and upheld this.
Although sentient beings lack Buddha-nature, [the teaching remains].
It should be upheld in this way:
for those sentient beings who have not yet possessed the causes for bodhi,
this sutra can open for them the great path to bodhi.
Thus it should be upheld.
For sentient beings who do not yet possess the radiance of the Dharma-body,
this sutra can provide them with the radiance of the Dharma-body.
Thus should it be upheld.
For those sentient beings who have not yet attained the conditions for samādhi,
this sutra can open for them the great gate of samādhi.
It should be upheld in this way:
for those sentient beings who have not yet reached nirvāṇa,
this sutra can enable them to attain nirvāṇa.
It should be upheld in this manner.
Although sentient beings may lack faith,
this sutra can bestow [benefit] upon them.
It eliminates the heavy sins of immeasurable and boundless birth and death,
with the exception of those who hold to the one-sided view (icchantika). Thus should it be upheld.
This sutra can deliver one from the sufferings of the eight difficulties;
it should be received and upheld in this manner.
This sutra can close the gates of the great hells for all sentient beings.
Receive and uphold it thus:
this sutra can enable sentient beings to destroy the four māras of affliction.
Receive and uphold it thus.
This sutra can serve as a great and wondrous medicine for sentient beings;
it should be received and upheld in this way.
This sutra can eliminate the disease of afflictions for sentient beings.
Receive and uphold it thus:
this sutra can encompass all sentient beings.
Receive and uphold it thus.
This sutra can eliminate harmful ghosts and spirits that injure others, and it utterly destroys the four directions so that all may be secure and at peace.
One should receive and uphold it in this manner.
Thus spoke the Buddha to the Bodhisattva Sāgarabuddhi.
"As for what you have just asked regarding the name by which this sutra should be known,
its meaning is exactly as I have explained it.
At that time, the Bodhisattva Sāgarabuddhivikrīḍita addressed the Buddha, saying:
World-Honored One,
we receive your venerable instruction upon our heads.
Indeed, World-Honored One.
"There are sentient beings who engage in much slander.
What will become of such people in the future?
The Buddha told Sāgarabuddhi:
In the future, there may be bhikṣus, bhikṣuṇīs, upāsakas, or upāsikās in Jambudvīpa who,
upon seeing someone reading or reciting this sutra,
will give rise to mutual anger and harbor slanderous intentions.
This is to slander the true Dharma.
For this reason, such a person will, within their current lifetime, encounter various evil and grave illnesses and will have incomplete physical faculties.

Or they may suffer from deafness, blindness, muteness, chronic abdominal disorders, possession by ghosts, possession by malevolent spirits, possession by evil influences, insanity, wind-disorders, cold-disorders, heat-disorders, hemorrhoids, edema, swellings, or the loss of mental faculties due to confusion.
Such various grave and evil illnesses as these remain in their bodies life after life;
thus they bring about suffering,
such that they find no peace whether sitting or lying down.
Feces do not pass;
urine does not flow;
one seeks life but cannot find it.
They seek death but cannot obtain it;
because they have slandered this sutra, they suffer in such a manner.
At times, they even die and fall further into the hells.
For eighty thousand kalpas they shall undergo great suffering and affliction;
for hundreds of thousands of millions of lifetimes, they shall never even hear the name of external food.
Such is the offense incurred by slandering this sutra.
At times they may even attain birth among human beings;
yet as oxen, horses, pigs, or sheep, they will be slaughtered by others and undergo extreme suffering.
Because they slandered this sutra, they undergo such suffering.
Furthermore, they will always be reborn in lower realms;
for hundreds of thousands of millions of lifetimes, they shall not attain autonomy.
Because they slandered this sutra, they undergo suffering such as this.
After dying from this state and returning to the human realm,
for hundreds of thousands of millions of lifetimes they shall never even hear the names of the Triple Gem;
because they slandered this sutra, they undergo suffering such as this.
Therefore, I tell you:
do not speak of this sutra among those who lack wisdom;
if they hear it, they will not understand it.
Do not speak to them either.
Only to those who possess right contemplation and right mindfulness should you then speak.
They constantly dwell in empty mountains,
remaining far removed from the five desires;
it is to such persons as these that you should then preach this.
If you see someone who is filial toward their parents and respectful toward their teachers and monks,
only then should you preach to such a person.
If you see someone who possesses loving-kindness, compassion, sympathetic joy, and equanimity, and makes offerings to the Buddhas, [then you may preach].
To such persons as these, one should then preach it.
If one sees someone whose heart is filled with joy and who respects śramaṇas,
whether they be great or small.
Virtue and non-virtue;
the Way and non-Way;
the Dharma and non-Dharma.
The mental conduct of the true practitioners and pure-faith women who read and recite this sutra and disseminate this sutra.
Revere this sutra;
do not slander this sutra;
have faith and delight in this sutra.
To those who make offerings to this sutra and who,
by reason of this, possess faith and reverence,
I shall from this day forth cause twenty-five bodhisattvas to protect and sustain them.
May this person always be free from illness and affliction;
may no malevolent spirits or ghosts harm them,
nor cause them any distress.
They shall not encounter misfortune;
they shall not behold evil;
nor shall they die an untimely death.
May this person always sleep in peace, dream in peace, awaken in peace, rise in peace, stand in peace, and walk in peace;
wherever this person goes, may they everywhere attain peace.
Furthermore, if there should be anyone who reads and recites this sutra,
they should maintain right mindfulness.
One should first contemplate repaying the Buddha’s kindness,
and only then explain it to others,
so that both the speaker and the listener may give rise to wholesome states of mind.
Those who love to preach this sutra—
both preacher and listener— shall all be reborn in the land of Amitābha.
Those who do not respect this sutra, its preacher, or its listeners shall fall into hell.
When both speaker and listener respect one another, they shall attain right liberation.
In every lifetime and in every place throughout all their births, they shall never encounter the eight difficulties.
According to their vows, they shall be reborn in the Land of Amitābha.
At that time, as the World-Honored One was about to conclude his preaching of the sutra,
the great earth shook and he emitted a great radiance.
The light of deliverance reaches sentient beings;
it shines upward upon the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven and downward upon the eighteen hells.
All hungry ghosts were completely liberated,
with the exception of those who hold one-sided views (icchantikas).
At the time he emitted light, ten billion worlds— blue, yellow, red, and white— were all blended into a golden color.
The people of Jambudvīpa all saw the emanated Buddha seated upon a precious lotus flower.
At that time, eighty-four thousand people of Jambudvīpa were all reborn in the heavens;
eighty-four thousand bhikṣus attained mastery of supernatural powers and the purity of the Dharma-eye.
Fourteen thousand śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas attained the first bhūmi;
eighty thousand bodhisattvas, as numerous as the sands of the Ganges, attained the fourth bhūmi;
and ten times the sands of the Ganges of great bodhisattvas attained the stage of non-retrogression and immovability.
At that time, the Brahma Kings and the Four Heavenly Kings all spoke these words:
"The Buddhas are difficult to encounter.
They then proceeded together to the place where the Buddha was.
Then, prostrating with his head at the Buddha's feet,
he said to the World-Honored One:
"We, too, shall now receive and uphold this sutra."
To protect all sentient beings,
the Buddha told the Four Heavenly Kings:
"You must now receive and uphold this sutra."
"I shall also cause all of you to be born in the Western Land of Amitābha in a future age.
He further addressed the twenty-five bodhisattvas:
"You, too, must now receive, uphold, and recite this sutra."
He spoke again to Ānanda:
"You all are my disciples of sharp wisdom;
after my parinirvāṇa, you shall receive, uphold, and recite this sutra."
For eighty thousand kalpas, it shall be widely proclaimed and disseminated,
so that throughout the Thousand Buddhas of the Bhadrakalpa, all sentient beings may universally hear and know it.
At that time, the World-Honored One spoke these words.
He withdrew the light.
The impurities of the earth, stones, and mountains of ten billion worlds were as they were before.
Thus the Buddha finished preaching the sutra.
The great bodhisattvas, śrāvakas, pratyekabuddhas, Ānanda,
and the entire assembly of the eight classes of gods and dragons paid homage with joy.
As taught, so one should practice.
Thus spoke the Buddha in the *Sāgarameghaprajñābodhisattvasūtra*.
